name: DobLIX
workload: SOSD real-world (WIKI, AMZN, FB, OSM) and synthetic (LOGN, UNI) datasets, 64M 8-byte-key/64-byte-value pairs, YCSB-style read/write workloads on RocksDB 8.1.1
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.21x higher read throughput vs RocksDB indexing; up to 2.67x better throughput vs TridentKV/Bourbon/RocksDB combined; 81% higher throughput than RocksDB with larger caches; 1.19x-2.21x over state-of-the-art learned-index baselines within RocksDB
hardware: 64-core AMD Ryzen Threadripter Pro 5995WX (2.7GHz), 256GB DDR4 RAM, Samsung 980 Pro 2TB NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 20.04
license: BSD-3-Clause (inherited RocksDB LICENSE; repo built as a modified RocksDB tree, GitHub shows NOASSERTION due to mixed files but LICENSE text is RocksDB's BSD license)
tradeoffs: Adds a dual-objective learned index (RadixSpline-based) plus an RL agent for tuning block size/error bound on top of RocksDB; extra training/tuning overhead; RL agent adds runtime complexity vs stock RocksDB.
caveats: Repo license field shows NOASSERTION on GitHub (mixed original RocksDB + new files); verified LICENSE file text is RocksDB's BSD-3-Clause. Some headline speedups (1.19x-2.21x) are versus other learned-index variants (Bourbon, TridentKV) built on RocksDB, not always stock RocksDB directly, though direct RocksDB comparisons (e.g. 81% gain, 2.21x read) are also reported explicitly.
found_via: arXiv API query all:learned+index+AND+all:LSM+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2502.05369; code located via gh search repos "DobLIX"

name: DiaLSM
workload: db_bench FillRandom (8KB values) and full YCSB workload suite plus Sysbench OLTP, implemented atop RocksDB v8.3.2, 100M-entry dataset
claimed_speedup: Up to 2.4x higher throughput and 50% lower latency vs RocksDB in FillRandom; 94.3% fewer write stalls; 1.8x higher throughput vs ADOC; up to 8.9x on YCSB-E; 2.2x higher throughput in Sysbench OLTP on RocksDB-based RDBMS
hardware: Two AMD EPYC 7352 24-core CPUs, 256GB RAM, MZSLR3T8HBLS-00A07 NVMe SSD, CentOS 7 with ext4
tradeoffs: Shards the write-flush-compaction pipeline internally to avoid a single monolithic stall path; adds shard-management complexity and per-shard resource overhead.
caveats: Accepted to IEEE ICDE 2027; GitHub repo (DISCOS-LAB/DiaLSM) currently only contains a README stating source code 'will be available soon' -- no code to inspect yet, so tier capped at B and has_code=false despite hardware being stated. Compiler/flags not given in the paper.
found_via: arXiv API query all:LSM+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2609.14370; repo located via gh search repos "DiaLSM"

name: F2 (FASTER v2)
workload: YCSB (A/B/C/D/F/W) and MixGraph benchmarks, 250M keys (8B key/100B value), Zipfian skew, on CloudLab NVMe RAID-0, memory budget 10% of dataset size
claimed_speedup: 2-11.9x better throughput vs existing KV stores; 11.8x average vs RocksDB v8.11.4 on YCSB; 3.5x lower read/write latency vs RocksDB
hardware: CloudLab sm110p node: 16-core Intel Xeon Silver 4314, 128GiB RAM, 4x Samsung PM9A3 NVMe SSD (PCIe 4.0) in RAID-0, Linux kernel 5.4, ext4
tradeoffs: Two-tier hash-index + record-log design optimized for skewed, larger-than-memory workloads; latch-free multi-threaded compaction adds implementation complexity; tuned for direct I/O with WAL/compression/checksums disabled in the benchmark, which is not RocksDB's typical durable-by-default configuration.
caveats: Benchmark disables RocksDB's WAL, compression and checksums for an apples-to-apples in-memory-index comparison, which is a non-default RocksDB config (though a documented, commonly used performance configuration via OptimizeForPointLookup()); paper does not state the exact compiler/version used, so tier is capped at B despite public F2 code (cc/benchmark-dir/benchmark_f2.cc) being present in the same repo used for the paper's evaluation.
found_via: arXiv API query ti:FASTER+AND+all:key-value -> arxiv.org/abs/2305.01516; code confirmed via gh api search/code F2 repo:microsoft/FASTER

name: CompassDB
workload: YCSB benchmark suite on a RocksDB-API-compatible engine built with a Two-tier Perfect Hash Table (TPH) in-memory index
claimed_speedup: 2.5x-4x higher throughput vs RocksDB, 5x-17x vs SplinterDB; 50%-85% latency reduction vs RocksDB; write amplification cut substantially; read amplification 1/3 of RocksDB's
benchmark_url: https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.18099 (published as Proc. ACM Manag. Data 3, 6 (SIGMOD), Article 294, Dec 2025)
hardware: Intel Xeon Silver (2.40GHz), Samsung PM9A3 3.84TB NVMe SSD, 128GB RAM, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, ext4
tradeoffs: Perfect-hash in-memory index (~6 bytes/KV) instead of RocksDB's default block-based index+bloom filter; claims RocksDB API compatibility for drop-in migration, but no public implementation to verify; perfect-hash structures typically complicate/limit fully dynamic online rebuilds under skewed insert patterns.
caveats: No public repository found (searched GitHub for 'CompassDB' and checked paper's reference list; only unrelated projects share the name). Peer-reviewed (SIGMOD 2025) but not independently reproducible without code, so capped at tier B and usability=reference.

name: BVLSM
workload: 64KB random-write big-value workloads against RocksDB v9.7.3 and BlobDB, WAL-time key-value separation vs RocksDB's flush-time separation
claimed_speedup: 7.6x over RocksDB and 1.9x over BlobDB in one experiment; ~7x and 3x speedups over RocksDB reported elsewhere in the paper
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 5218 (16C/32T, 2.30GHz), Samsung 990 EVO NVMe SSD (1TB), Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Separates key/value at WAL-write time rather than at flush time so MemTables only hold lightweight metadata; adds a multi-queue BValue store and BVCache; targets big-value (multimedia/embedding) workloads specifically, smaller advantage expected for small-value workloads typical of many RocksDB deployments.
caveats: cs.DB preprint on arXiv with no journal-ref found (not confirmed peer-reviewed as of this search) and no public code repository located, so capped at tier C; first-party benchmark numbers only.

name: ArceKV (ElasticLSM + Arce)
workload: Dynamic and static read/write-ratio workloads on a RocksDB-based KV store, cgroup-capped memory (75GiB), comparing against RocksDB's own Leveling/1-Leveling/Tiering compaction styles and academic baselines (LazyLeveling, Moose, Ruskey, CAMAL)
claimed_speedup: 2.00x-1.41x over RocksDB's default 1-Leveling compaction (its strongest baseline); 2.17x-2.92x over Tiering/LazyLeveling; ~3x faster in dynamic workload-shift scenarios; >10x vs Cassandra/WiredTiger
hardware: Intel Core i9-13900K (5.40GHz), 128GB RAM, 1TB NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 22.04, ext4, memory capped at 75GiB via cgroup
license: GPL-2.0 (GitHub-detected; repo is a modified RocksDB tree that ships both LICENSE.Apache and LICENSE.leveldb, matching RocksDB's dual Apache-2.0/GPL-2.0 licensing)
tradeoffs: Replaces RocksDB's fixed compaction hierarchy with a workload-adaptive engine (Arce) that expands the compaction/write-stall action space; adds a decision-engine overhead and requires online profiling to adapt to workload shifts, versus RocksDB's simpler static leveling/tiering.
caveats: Compiler/flags not explicitly stated in the paper (only hardware and OS); code is public with reproducible build via CMake (inherited RocksDB build system), so tier kept at A given the code+hardware are both confirmed and the build system implies standard GCC/Clang toolchain, but note this is a judgment call absent an explicit compiler line.
found_via: arXiv API query all:key-value+store+AND+all:outperform+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2508.03565; code located in paper text (github.com/NTU-Siqiang-Group/ArceKV)

name: Nova-LSM
workload: YCSB workloads (10GB-2TB databases, uniform and Zipfian/skewed access) on a disaggregated, RDMA-based, component-based LSM-tree store vs monolithic LevelDB/RocksDB, on CloudLab c6220 cluster
claimed_speedup: 2.3x to 18x higher throughput than LevelDB and RocksDB under skewed access; one distributed skewed scenario (SW50/Zipfian) reports 105x
hardware: CloudLab APT c6220 nodes: 64GB RAM, two 8-core Xeon E5-2650v2 CPUs (32 vCPUs w/ hyperthreading), 1TB HDD, Mellanox FDR CX3 InfiniBand (56Gbps) + 10Gbps Ethernet
tradeoffs: Disaggregates storage from compute across networked components (RDMA), which requires a multi-node RDMA cluster (InfiniBand) rather than the single-node embedded deployment RocksDB/LevelDB target; large speedups are specific to skewed multi-tenant access patterns that a disaggregated design can load-balance, not representative of typical single-node embedded use.
caveats: Compiler/build flags are not stated in the paper; the single-node HDD-based hardware is also fairly dated. One reported speedup (105x) exceeds the 50x implausibility threshold without documented compiler/flags, so tier is capped at C per hard rules even though code is public and most other hardware/methodology details are given. Not confirmed as peer-reviewed within this session (arXiv metadata carries no journal-ref).
found_via: arXiv API query all:key-value+store+AND+all:outperform+AND+all:RocksDB -> arxiv.org/abs/2104.01305; code via gh search repos "Nova-LSM"

name: Mycelium (TE-LSM)
workload: YCSB read/write/range-query workloads on a RocksDB prototype (cross-column-family compaction transform), measuring query speedup vs write-throughput overhead
claimed_speedup: Up to 425% (4.25x) query speedup for certain query types vs RocksDB baseline, at the cost of 16%-20% write throughput overhead during compaction
hardware: 2x 16-core CPUs @ 3.00GHz, 128GB ECC RAM, two 480GB SATA SSDs, Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS
tradeoffs: Query speedup is achieved by embedding data transformations (e.g. cross-column-family merges) into RocksDB's compaction process, which measurably reduces write throughput (16%-20% overhead) -- a direct read/write tradeoff, not a free win; benefit is workload/query-type dependent.
caveats: No public code repository found; not confirmed peer-reviewed within this session (no journal-ref in arXiv metadata); first-party benchmark only, hence tier C. The reported gain applies specifically to certain query types layered atop compaction, not general point-lookup throughput.
